title: The Symbolic Ape
text:
Blombos Cave
How chemistry became civilization
Look around you.
Cities.
Money.
Governments.
Markets.
Algorithms.
Religions.
Art.
War.
All of it began with a strange evolutionary event: a primate species learned how to think in symbols.
Humans are, biologically speaking, apes.
But we are symbolic apes.
And once that ability emerged, everything changed.
Reality did not start with meaning
At the foundation of reality there is no meaning.
There is only physics.
Energy moves through the universe following the laws of thermodynamics.
Stars form.
Planets cool.
Chemical reactions occur.
Over immense stretches of time, some chemical systems begin to organize themselves in unusual ways.
Life appears.
Life is essentially matter that temporarily resists entropy.
Cells maintain structure.
They repair themselves.
They harvest energy from their surroundings.
But even here there is still no meaning.
There is only persistence.
Life becomes predictive
As organisms become more complex, they develop nervous systems.
A nervous system is fundamentally a prediction engine.
It constantly estimates:
Where food might be
Where danger might appear
How the environment is changing.
The organisms that predict better survive more often.
Over millions of years nervous systems become increasingly sophisticated. They begin modeling not just the outside world, but the internal state of the body as well.
The organism is no longer merely reacting.
It is anticipating.
This is the beginning of cognition.
The expensive brain
Human cognition did not evolve for free.
The human brain consumes roughly 20 percent of the body’s energy, despite representing only a small fraction of body mass.
For such a costly organ to evolve, something had to change in the human energy economy.
Several developments likely made this possible:
Cooperative hunting
Food sharing within social groups
Richer diets
And perhaps most importantly, cooking.
Cooking breaks down food and releases more calories. Fire effectively increased the amount of usable energy available to the human body.
With more energy available, brains could grow.
And once brains reached a certain threshold of complexity, something remarkable appeared.
The symbolic leap
Roughly forty to fifty thousand years ago, the archaeological record begins to change.
Humans start producing objects that have no direct survival function:
Cave paintings
Carved figurines
Musical instruments
Personal ornaments
Abstract markings.
These artifacts appear in sites such as Chauvet Cave and other Paleolithic locations across Eurasia.
They represent something new.
A painted animal is not the animal itself.
A carved figure may represent a spirit or mythic being.
A symbol stands for something else.
This is the moment when humans begin living inside a second world.
A symbolic world.
Living in two realities
From this point onward humans inhabit two overlapping layers of reality.
The first is the physical world:
bodies, ecosystems, weather, and energy flows.
The second is the symbolic world:
language, stories, laws, identities, myths, and institutions.
These symbolic systems allow humans to coordinate behavior across groups far larger than any other primate species.
Tribes form around shared stories.
Norms regulate behavior.
Rituals reinforce identity.
Over time these symbolic structures become increasingly powerful.
They give rise to:
Religion
Political institutions
Economic systems
Science
Technological innovation.
Civilization itself is essentially a symbolic coordination system built on top of biology.
Complexity scales upward
Once symbolic cognition appears, cultural knowledge begins accumulating across generations.
Each generation inherits tools, techniques, stories, and rules.
Small groups become villages.
Villages become cities.
Cities develop trade networks.
Technology evolves.
Economic systems organize resources.
Institutions govern large populations.
New layers of abstraction appear:
laws, markets, bureaucracies, algorithms.
Each layer builds upon the layers beneath it.
Biology enables cognition.
Cognition enables symbols.
Symbols enable civilization.
The strange power of symbols
Symbols allow humans to coordinate behavior around things that do not physically exist.
Money works because people collectively believe in it.
Nations exist because people share a story about belonging.
Legal systems function because societies agree to follow symbolic rules.
These symbolic structures can become immensely powerful.
They mobilize armies.
They organize economies.
They reshape landscapes.
In many ways, human civilization is the result of imagined systems acting on the physical world.
The question of meaning
At the lowest layers of reality, meaning does not exist.
Physics does not ask why.
Biology does not search for purpose.
But once symbolic cognition emerges, humans begin asking questions that no other species appears to ask.
Why are we here?
What should we do with the power we have created?
What kind of world should we build?
Ethical systems and spiritual traditions emerge partly as attempts to answer those questions.
They attempt to regulate the symbolic ape.
The creature we have become
Seen from a distance, humanity is a remarkable evolutionary experiment.
A primate species developed the ability to represent reality with symbols.
Those symbols built cultures.
Those cultures built civilizations.
Those civilizations now operate systems of enormous scale: financial networks, technological infrastructures, global institutions.
And increasingly, machines that process symbols faster than we can.
We are still biological organisms resisting entropy for a brief moment in time.
But we are also something unprecedented.
A species that builds worlds out of imagination.
The symbolic ape.
The story of humanity is not simply the story of intelligence.
It is the story of symbols.
Symbols allowed a primate species to build myths, religions, sciences, and civilizations.
They allowed us to coordinate millions of people who will never meet.
They allowed us to imagine futures that do not yet exist.
But symbols are powerful tools.
They can build meaning, art, and knowledge.
They can also produce ideologies, bureaucracies, and systems that become detached from the reality they were meant to represent.
The symbolic ape lives between these two possibilities.
Creation and confusion.
Meaning and illusion.
And the future of our species may depend on whether we learn to tell the difference.

title: Hatred is a feedback loop (and the Qur’an names the constraint that breaks it)
text:
In the past weeks, violence has repeatedly spilled out beyond formal battlefields.
A reported shooting at a synagogue is not “separate” from the wider atmosphere. When Gaza dominates the moral imagination, and when the Iran question keeps tightening regional tension, fear and outrage travel fast.
At the same time, trust in governments and institution s is degrading. Many people no longer expect public authority to tell the truth, act proportionally, or protect civilian life. In that vacuum, anger becomes socially contagious, and identity becomes the nearest available target.
Hatred rarely arrives as an ideology first.
It arrives as a sequence.
Something harmful happens. Anger rises. Anger hardens into hatred. Hatred turns people into symbols. Symbols become targets. The next harm is then framed as “justice,” which generates the next wave of anger.
That is a feedback loop.
In systems terms, the output of the system (retaliation) becomes the input that amplifies the original signal (harm). The loop does not naturally stabilize. It escalates, spreads, and recruits bystanders.
The loop in one line
Harm → anger → hatred → dehumanization → moral permission for injustice → new harm.
The Qur’an does not deny that anger exists after injury. It treats anger as a human signal.
What it regulates is what humans do with the signal, because unbounded anger becomes a generator of new injustice.
Anger vs hatred: signal vs identity
One clarification matters.
Anger can be a morally meaningful response to real harm. It can alert you that something is wrong and motivate repair.
Hatred is different. Hatred is an identity state. It reorganizes perception.
It collapses individuals into a category.
It narrows moral imagination.
It makes cruelty feel like coherence.
In a loop, hatred functions like a high-gain amplifier: it increases the intensity and the scope of response beyond the original event.
The Qur’anic constraint that blocks escalation
One of the Qur’an’s clearest “circuit breakers” is this:
“O you who believe. Stand firmly for Allah as witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people cause you to act unjustly. Be just; that is closer to righteousness.”
Once such a loop begins, it can escalate far beyond the original event.
— Qur’an 5:8
The verse does not pretend hatred will never arise.
It assumes it can arise.
But it insists on a hard boundary:
Justice must not become a function of hatred.
The presence of hostility does not grant moral license.
In other words, the Qur’an separates two things that human beings constantly try to fuse:
I feel justified.
I am just.
A feedback loop is often powered by that fusion.
“Repel evil with what is better” is a claim about dynamics, not passivity
Another Qur’anic instruction is often misunderstood as sentimental.
It is better read as an insight into escalation.
“Repel evil with what is better. Then the one between whom and you was hostility may become as though they were a devoted friend.”
Modern science offers another way to understand the same phenomenon.
— Qur’an 41:34
This is not a denial of conflict.
It is a refusal to reproduce conflict’s internal logic.
In systems language: when an interaction is locked into a loop, repeating the same input produces the same outcome. Changing the input can change the trajectory. Sometimes it breaks the loop. Sometimes it reveals the other party’s intent more clearly. In either case, it prevents your own moral center from being hijacked by the loop.
Collective blame: the shortcut that makes cruelty “thinkable”
Hatred spreads fastest when responsibility becomes collective.
A government’s actions become “what that people are.”
A militant group becomes “what that religion is.”
A crime becomes “what that community deserves.”
This shortcut is psychologically efficient, and morally catastrophic.
The Qur’an rejects this directly:
“No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another.”
— Qur’an 6:164
Once societies abandon this principle, collective punishment becomes imaginable, and then increasingly normal.
Conflict is real, but it must remain bounded
The Qur’an is not utopian about history. It recognizes struggle and power.
“If Allah did not restrain some people by means of others, the earth would be filled with corruption.”
Hatred is a form of social disorder energy. When it spreads unchecked, institutions weaken, trust collapses, and collective stability deteriorates.
— Qur’an 2:251
This verse is not romantic. It describes a world where power contests exist.
But it implies something crucial: the world remains inhabitable because constraints exist.
Restraint is not weakness. Restraint is a stabilizing mechanism.
Fasād: when conflict turns into systemic destruction
The Qur’an’s concept of fasād is not only personal immorality. It is social and ecological breakdown: the destruction of life-support systems.
“When he turns away, he strives throughout the land to spread corruption and destroy crops and lives. And Allah does not love corruption.”
entire populations
— Qur’an 2:205
In modern terms, fasād is what happens when violence is no longer only an act, but becomes an environment.
Trust decays. Institutions weaken. Norms collapse. Families fracture. The capacity to think clearly disappears.
Hatred accelerates this process because it makes destruction feel righteous.
A brief note on self-defense and limits
Ethical restraint is not the same as surrender.
The Qur’an contains permissions and limits around self-defense and conflict.
But even where force is permitted, the Qur’anic project remains the same:
Do not let rage become your law
Do not let identity become a target
Do not let injustice become your method
Because once injustice becomes your method, you have already entered the loop.
The political layer: why this spreads globally now
Modern media networks act like accelerants.
Images of suffering travel instantly. Moral emotions spread faster than analysis. People are recruited into simplified narratives before they have time to reflect.
In such conditions, hatred becomes contagious. It jumps across borders and lands on nearby identities.
A faraway conflict becomes an excuse for local violence.
People who had nothing to do with a decision become symbols for it.
That is the signature of a feedback loop: the system expands beyond its initial boundary.
Breaking the loop: what the Qur’an actually demands
The Qur’an’s contribution here is not an abstract moral aesthetic. It is a practical constraint designed to prevent moral collapse under pressure.
Justice is independent of hatred. (5:8)
Better response can change the trajectory. (41:34)
Individuals are not interchangeable with their group. (6:164)
Restraint is part of why the world remains habitable. (2:251)
Corruption includes systemic destruction of life. (2:205)
The real question
The hardest question in periods of conflict is not “Who is angry?”
Anger will exist.
The hard question is: Will anger be used to protect justice, or to permit injustice?
Because hatred feels like clarity.
But in a loop, hatred is not clarity.
Hatred is fuel.
Reflective questions
Where do I confuse “I feel justified” with “I am being just”?
What identities do I collapse into symbols when I am emotionally flooded?
What would it mean for me to hold one ethical constraint steady even under pressure?
What would “repel with what is better” look like in one specific interaction this week?
Where am I tempted by collective blame because it is cognitively easier than careful responsibility?
If I wanted to reduce fasād rather than amplify it, what would I stop sharing, stop saying, or stop excusing today?

title: Honest Islam Exploration
text:
March 15 – April 15, 2026
Hello everyone,
It has been a while since I wrote something this personal.
Life has been full. I have been working as a nurse, staying engaged with “De Nieuwe Vredesbeweging”, and trying to find my role in the peace movement while continuing my systems research. Alongside all of that, I have been doing something more quiet but more daily: building steady contact with the Qur’an, and letting Islamic practice begin to structure my days.
I want to be honest about where I am coming from.
I grew up in a non‑religious, Western, liberal environment. Religion was never central to my identity or my routines. But over the past months, the Qur’an has been changing the way I see reality.
Probably not in the way many people expect.
What I have actually been doing (not just thinking)
This is not a declaration of arrival. It is a record of practice.
Daily Qur’an contact: tilāwah, pronunciation work, and slow reading. I keep notes and reflections as I go.
Tafsīr and meaning-building: I am trying to understand what the text is saying on its own terms, not through inherited culture-war frames.
Embodied practice experiments: building a morning foundation sequence (purification → Qur’an contact → dhikr → prayer), and learning basics like wuḍūʾ carefully.
Ethical and character orientation: treating Islam less as “belief content” and more as a training system for humility, responsibility, and constraint.
Specific theme inquiries: for example, exploring modesty and hijab as an inside–outside feedback loop (intention → outward practice → inner state), rather than a cosmetic rule or a social performance.
If you have followed my writing for a while, you will recognize this pattern: I do not trust conclusions that are not backed by lived testing. I am trying to bring that same discipline here.
Why Islam fits the systems lens (and also corrects it)
What I have discovered is that the structure, practices, and orientation of Islam form a kind of architecture.
From a systems perspective, it looks like a set of repeated, embodied interventions that shape the self over time:
The self is not sovereign.
The self is embedded in forces it cannot fully perceive or control.
Agency exists, but it exists within bounds: constrained, limited, dependent.
Scary, perhaps.
Or maybe simply natural.
Did you come into existence entirely by yourself?
Did you build the conditions of your own life without help from countless processes you do not fully understand?
Probably not.
And that realization changes how you see freedom, responsibility, and humility.
Islam, at least as I am encountering it right now, does not flatter the modern self. It re-centers something else: accountability, discipline, worship, and a long time-horizon.
Misconceptions and the reason I am writing openly
There are many misconceptions about Islam. Some come from outside the religion. Some come from within it.
But this is not unique to Islam. The same thing happens in Christianity, Buddhism, Judaism, and secular ideological communities.
It is a very human phenomenon.
I am also aware that I do not fully understand Islam. In fact, I am completely certain that I never will fully understand anything.
That realization comes with studying perception itself.
Human perception is limited. It is functional, relational, and dependent. What we experience is never completely “direct.” It emerges through relationships, feedback loops, and interaction with the world around us.
In that sense, the human being is also a feedback system:
aware
sometimes stubborn
capable of choice
We can resist.
We can wander.
But we can also return.
Religious traditions describe this as staying on a straight path: adopting practices that shape the self over time. Practices refined and lived for centuries, aimed at producing moral individuals and sustainable societies.
What this series is
For that reason, I have decided to explore Islam seriously.
Not a little.
Not halfway.
But as a lived exploration, allowing its practices, discipline, and orientation to shape my life and my thinking.
I wondered for a while whether I should explore this privately. In the end, I decided to do it openly.
Because I think the structure of what Islam has been, historically, intellectually, and spiritually, is worth examining honestly.
But I also want to keep the frame clean:
I will distinguish observation from interpretation, and practice from performance.
I will not write as if certainty has been achieved when what I actually have is a series of experiments.
When I am unsure, I will say so.
This series is not a declaration of certainty.
It is an exploration.
And like all honest exploration, it begins with humility.

title: Modern Society: A Systems Diagnosis
text:
Modern society is not simply “declining.”
It is simultaneously more capable than any society in history and, in many ways, less coherent than many that came before.
We have unprecedented technological power, material abundance, and global connectivity. Yet we also see falling birth rates, rising chronic illness, declining trust in institutions, widespread psychological strain, and a growing loss of shared meaning.
That combination can look like a contradiction. Structurally, it is not. It is what happens when a system optimizes aggressively for capability, control, efficiency, speed, and choice, while quietly degrading the conditions that make complexity sustainable: shared orientation, social coordination, and inner regulation.
Here is the diagnosis in one line:
High complexity with low coherence produces instability.
To see why, you have to look across layers. Not just politics or economics, but meaning, institutions, incentives, attention, bodies, and the physical limits underneath everything.
Capability up, coherence down
Modernity scales upward brilliantly. It can coordinate global supply chains, produce advanced medicine, standardize laws, and distribute information at planetary speed.
What it struggles to do is stabilize downward: the moral, social, cognitive, and biological foundations that allow ordinary people to coordinate over time.
When the foundation weakens, a society can still look powerful for a while. But it becomes brittle.
Brittleness is not the same as weakness. It is what you get when a system has a lot of power but little resilience, when it cannot absorb shocks without fracturing.
Meaning: pluralism without a shared horizon
Earlier societies typically carried a built-in answer to a question modern life often cannot hold steady:
What is a good life?
Historically, the answer was not only private. It was socially reinforced. Whether religious or civic, a shared moral framework created a hierarchy of values and a sense of duty beyond preference.
Modern societies replaced much of that with pluralism and self-definition. Meaning becomes a personal project.
That shift increases freedom. It also makes collective coordination harder. Large-scale systems do not run on individual preference alone. They require some shared “north star”, a horizon that makes sacrifice in the present feel legitimate in service of a future the collective still trusts.
When no common moral horizon exists, responsibility becomes negotiable, identity becomes unstable, and long-term commitments weaken. A society can tolerate disagreement. What it cannot tolerate indefinitely is the absence of any binding frame that legitimizes coordination.
Institutions: governance without trust turns into enforcement
Modern states and institutions have extraordinary administrative capacity. They can regulate industries, maintain legal continuity, and coordinate complex infrastructure.
Yet legitimacy, felt trust, has been eroding.
When a population no longer shares basic priorities, institutions are asked to govern a field of conflict rather than a shared culture. The predictable result is more bureaucracy, more procedural complexity, more short-term policy churn, and a growing perception that institutions are detached from real human life.
As trust declines, the system compensates with rules.
Rules can maintain order. They cannot produce legitimacy. Over time, governance drifts from coordination toward enforcement.
Incentives: a machine that rewards outputs, not human continuity
Modern economies are astonishing at optimizing for productivity, growth, and efficiency.
But human beings do not optimize on those variables. Human systems require stability, continuity, health, and relational depth.
When incentives cut against these needs, people do not become “better.” They adapt rationally.
This is one reason birth rates fall. In many modern contexts, children become an economic risk rather than an embedded value. Housing and long-term security feel inaccessible. The cultural scaffolding that makes sacrifice meaningful weakens. People delay commitment because the system punishes commitment.
Life becomes transactional: a series of negotiations with a machine whose outputs are measurable, but whose ends are unclear.
Technology: an attention ecology optimized for engagement, not depth
Technology increases capability and convenience. It also changes the information environment faster than the human organism can adapt.
Most dominant platforms optimize for engagement, speed, and scale.
They do not optimize for truth, coherence, or psychological stability.
So attention fragments. People live in near-constant stimulation. Depth becomes rare.
This is not merely a cultural complaint. It is a systems problem. When attention is repeatedly broken, higher-order coordination becomes harder both internally (within a person) and externally (between people). A society cannot stay coherent if its members cannot sustain focus long enough to form stable judgments or commitments.
Social structure: atomization at scale
Large-scale urban systems can be materially efficient. They can also be socially thin.
Modern life often produces high anonymity, weak community bonds, and low accountability. People live near each other, but not with each other.
Social cohesion is not an abstract moral ideal. It is a practical stabilizer. Humans regulate through repeated interaction, shared norms, and mutual recognition.
When those weaken, loneliness rises, distrust rises, and public life becomes more easily polarized.
Information: competing realities replace shared truth
Modern societies once relied on common epistemic anchors: institutions and norms that made truth disputes narrower and slower.
Now narratives multiply endlessly, authority is contested by default, and algorithms separate people into parallel streams.
Over time, this does not merely produce disagreement. It produces incompatible realities.
When there is no shared reality, large-scale coordination fails. Trust becomes impossible because people cannot even agree on what is happening.
The nervous system: dysregulation becomes the baseline
A chronically stressed population becomes reactive, exhausted, and less able to think long-term.
Modern life contains constant stimulation, economic pressure, social uncertainty, and weakened grounding structures.
The result is widespread dysregulation: anxiety, burnout, and a chronic sense of unsafety.
This matters because a dysregulated nervous system struggles to sustain meaning, discipline, patience, or coherent social behavior.
When the nervous system destabilizes, everything above it becomes harder to maintain.
Biology and ecology: the floor you cannot negotiate with
At the base are constraints.
Bodies have limits. Sleep has limits. Metabolic health has limits. So do ecosystems. Soil depletes. Biodiversity collapses. Energy is constrained by thermodynamics.
No ideology overrides physical reality.
A civilization can build impressive systems for a time while degrading its biological and ecological base. Eventually, the base layer asserts itself.
Complexity requires healthy organisms living within regenerating environments.
So what is actually happening?
Modern society has achieved extraordinary capability without maintaining alignment.
It scaled complexity without stabilizing coherence.
That is why we get the strange condition of immense power paired with fragile meaning, eroded trust, fragmented attention, and dysregulated bodies.
The system did not fail because it became weak.
It became powerful without staying coherent.
What would restore coherence?
If the problem is high complexity plus low coherence, the solution is not “more freedom” or “more control” alone.
It is re-alignment across layers, with real trade-offs.
A society needs a shared horizon that makes commitment intelligible. It needs institutions that can earn legitimacy, not merely enforce compliance. It needs incentives that reward human continuity rather than punish it. It needs an information environment that can sustain shared reality. It needs social structures that regenerate belonging and accountability. And it needs rhythms of life that restore nervous system stability rather than continuously violate it.
In other words: the future is not decided by technology alone. It is decided by whether human beings can rebuild the conditions for coherent coordination before the system loses the ability to coordinate itself.
A powerful society can survive many problems.
It cannot survive long with high capability and low coherence.
A reflective question
If coherence is the real scarce resource now, then what would you be willing to trade, personally or collectively, to rebuild it?

title: Iran War: What It Does to the World
subtitle: (and what it reveals about the system we live in)
text:
War is easy to keep at a distance.
If you stay on the surface, it looks like a world made of maps and statements. Leaders speak in careful language. Analysts talk about deterrence and red lines. The story feels contained.
But in real life, war does not stay on the map.
It moves through the world the way a shock moves through a body.
And one of the fastest ways it moves is through energy.
What is happening around Iran is often described as a regional escalation. In one sense, it is. But structurally, it is also something larger: a disturbance in the metabolic system of modern civilization.
That is why people who live far away still feel it.
Not because they have a strong opinion about the Middle East.
Because they live inside the same tightly coupled system.
War as an energy disturbance
Modern life rests on flows.
We tend to talk as if our societies are built on ideas, values, and institutions first. Those things matter. But they sit on top of something more basic.
They sit on energy.
Vaclav Smil has spent decades showing, in different ways, that complex societies rise and stabilize when they can reliably do three things: extract energy, convert it efficiently, and distribute it at scale. When that foundation is steady, everything above it can look smooth. When it is threatened, the smoothness disappears quickly.
That is not ideology.
It is physical constraint.
This is why a place like the Strait of Hormuz matters so much. It is not “just” a geographic detail. It is one of the world’s most critical chokepoints for oil shipments, and it sits inside a region that supplies a significant share of global petroleum. When conflict heightens in or near Iran, markets do not wait for certainty. They re-price risk.
And because energy prices ripple through almost everything, the shock does not remain “over there.”
Energy touches transport. Transport touches food. Food touches household budgets. Household pressure touches politics. None of this requires direct dependency. In a globally priced market, price coupling is enough.
In Europe, for example, gas and electricity prices can react sharply to geopolitical stress, even when the immediate supply routes are different, because expectations shift, storage levels matter, and countries compete for alternative supply. The Netherlands has seen this dynamic before. When storage is low after winter, sensitivity increases. A change in perceived risk can translate into real cost pressure.
The point is not that one event deterministically causes one price.
The point is that we are living inside a system where shocks travel fast.
What the global system actually is (beneath the narratives)
Most of us describe the world in narratives.
We say “capitalism,” “globalization,” “politics,” “the West,” “the Global South.” These words can be useful. But they often hide the mechanism.
Mechanically, the world economy behaves like a high-speed network designed for throughput.
Over decades, we optimized for efficiency: lean inventories, just-in-time delivery, long supply chains, rapid financial feedback, and tight integration across regions. The result is extraordinary productive power. But the trade-off is fragility.
A resilient system has slack. It has buffers. It can take a hit and localize the damage.
A highly optimized system tends to do the opposite. It transmits stress.
This is why “stability” can be misleading. What we call stability is often simply uninterrupted flow.
When the flow is uninterrupted, the system feels solid.
When the flow is threatened, we learn how quickly the surface calm depended on invisible coordination.
Five things this war reveals, more clearly
The first thing it reveals is the oldest lesson of all systems: efficiency and resilience are not the same goal.
Smil’s work, and the energy history behind it, makes this feel obvious. If you remove redundancy to maximize output and minimize cost, you also remove shock absorbers. When disruption comes, there is less capacity to adapt without pain.
That pain often arrives quietly at first, as a price signal. It shows up as higher heating costs, more expensive groceries, and rising transport costs. Then it becomes political.
The second thing it reveals is cascade risk.
Our system is not modular. It is tightly coupled. Energy feeds transport. Transport feeds supply chains. Supply chains feed food and consumer goods. Prices feed social mood. Social mood feeds governance.
In a modular system, a failure can remain local.
In a tightly coupled system, a disturbance propagates.
That is why a conflict near Iran can matter in a Dutch supermarket even if the Netherlands is not “directly” importing the same barrel of oil. The coupling is financial and logistical, not personal.
The third thing it reveals is about human behavior under stress.
Robert Sapolsky’s work is useful here because it pushes against a comforting myth: that people become more rational under pressure.
Often, the opposite happens.
Under uncertainty, perceived threat, and resource pressure, human beings tend to narrow. Attention shortens. Tribal instincts activate. People search for simple explanations and strong identities. This is not because people are foolish. It is because the human nervous system is not built to calmly track complex multi-variable systems while also feeling unsafe.
So systemic stress does not only degrade material conditions. It can also degrade cognitive conditions. Polarization rises. Coordination becomes harder. Outrage becomes a substitute for understanding.
The fourth thing it reveals is how quickly narratives replace models.
When reality becomes too complex to hold, people compress it. Multi-causal systems get reduced to single villains. Structural dynamics get turned into moral stories.
Again: not stupidity.
Constraint.
But the consequence is serious. If we cannot see the system accurately, we cannot regulate our own responses to it, and we cannot design policy that matches reality.
The fifth thing it reveals is a misalignment of timescales.
Most incentives in modern life run on short cycles: quarterly performance, election seasons, media attention, and immediate public mood. But the infrastructure that supports civilization runs on long cycles: energy investment, ecological stability, industrial capacity, and generational cohesion.
That mismatch creates drift.
War does not create the mismatch.
War simply exposes it.
Is this collapse?
“Collapse” is a powerful word, but it is often too coarse.
What we are seeing is better described as stress accumulation in a tightly coupled system.
The system is still functioning. Goods still move. Markets still clear. Institutions still operate.
But the weak points become visible under load.
This is why the Bronze Age comparison sometimes appears: interconnected networks, dependence on key nodes, fragility hidden by prior stability. The difference today is scale and speed. The network is global, and the feedback is near-instant.
So the question is not whether the world is “fine” or “doomed.”
The question is: how does a tightly coupled system behave when shocks become more frequent, and when buffers are thin?
What this means at the individual level (concrete, not performative)
It is easy to react to systemic stress in two extremes.
One is to say, “We must fix the whole system.”
The other is to say, “Nothing can be done.”
Both are incomplete.
You cannot personally control global energy flows or geopolitical decisions.
But you are not without agency.
You can change your position inside the system.
You can reduce fragility.
You can build margin.
You can protect attention and behavior so you do not become another unstable node.
One practical place to start is to look at dependency chains.
Most of us are more exposed to long chains than we realize. Food, heat, mobility, and basic household goods all run through energy-intensive logistics. You cannot opt out, but you can shorten where possible: know where essentials come from, diversify suppliers, and build a small amount of local capacity.
Even a small amount of food growing is not a lifestyle statement. It is a partial decoupling from a long chain.
Another place to start is buffers.
The modern system removed buffers because buffers look inefficient.
Do not copy that logic into personal life.
Financial margin. Stored essentials. Extra time in the week. A bit of redundancy in skills and relationships.
These are not dramatic preparations.
They are quiet resilience.
They are the difference between a shock becoming an inconvenience versus a crisis.
A third place is feedback with reality.
One of the strangest features of modern life is distance between action and consequence. We consume without seeing production. We speak without seeing impact. We outsource without understanding dependencies.
Rebuilding even a small amount of visible input → output process recalibrates the mind.
Food is one of the clearest arenas for this, but not the only one.
A fourth place is behavioral regulation.
Sapolsky’s most uncomfortable insight is also one of the most compassionate: behavior is context-dependent.
So do not rely only on identity and intention (“I am the kind of person who stays calm”).
Design the context.
Reduce unnecessary stressors where possible. Limit exposure to outrage cycles. Build routines that stabilize the nervous system. Make it easier to be the person you want to be when the environment becomes harsher.
And finally: act locally where action is real.
A system can feel abstract and ungraspable.
But suffering is never abstract.
Helping one person is not a solution to geopolitics.
But it is not nothing.
It is a real intervention in the only scale where morality is always concrete: person to person.
A different orientation
If there is a deeper layer beneath all this, it is not “war.”
It is orientation.
We built a world optimized for speed, scale, and efficiency.
We did not build it for coherence, stability, or alignment with human limits.
So people compensate: activism without structure, narratives without models, reaction without regulation.
That is why even movements that claim to seek peace can struggle to maintain peace internally.
They are operating from activation instead of structural understanding.
A diagnostic event, and a choice
The escalation around Iran is not just another headline.
It is a diagnostic event.
It shows where the system is tightly coupled.
It shows where buffers are thin.
It shows how quickly material stress becomes cognitive and political stress.
And it asks a more honest question than “How do we fix the world?”
It asks: how do we live inside this world without inheriting its fragility?
For me, this is part of why religious frameworks remain such powerful attractors. Not because they deny complexity, but because they offer stable orientation, repeated structure, and constraint on impulse. In a system that amplifies instability, that matters.
“Guide us on the straight path” is not abstract.
It is a request for alignment under conditions where misalignment is easy.
If this lens resonates, share this essay with someone who has been feeling the pressure but cannot name the mechanism. And if you want more writing like this, subscribe to The Living Fractal so you can follow the next pieces in this series, where I map the system more clearly and make the practical implications even more concrete.

title: When I’m menstruating: keeping orientation without ṣalāh (Eid Fajr edition)
text:
Photo by Damiano Baschiera on Unsplash
Eid mubārak.
If you are menstruating this morning and not praying Fajr, the absence can feel strangely sharp.
Not because you are “less Muslim,” and not because you are spiritually dirty, but because ṣalāh is a daily structure that holds the heart in place.
When that structure pauses, a very human question appears:
How do I stay oriented when my most familiar form of worship is temporarily not available?
What “Eid Fajr” means
Fajr is the dawn prayer.
Eid is the day of celebration that Allah gave the believers after a season of worship.
So when people say “Eid Fajr,” they mean the early morning of Eid, when many Muslims wake before sunrise, pray Fajr, and then prepare for the Eid prayer later that morning.
It is a morning that can feel unusually bright.
New clothes.
Food later.
Messages.
Family gatherings.
And also, often, a deep inner tenderness.
If you are not praying today because of ḥayḍ (menstruation), you are not “missing Islam.”
You are simply living one of the human states that Islam already accounts for.
What menstruation means in Islam (and what it does not mean)
In Islam, menstruation (ḥayḍ) is not treated as a moral stain.
It is not a sign that a woman is spiritually rejected.
It is not a reason for shame.
It is a physical state that changes certain acts of worship for a time.
For most women, this includes that ṣalāh is paused during menstruation, and fasting is made up later.
This is not because worship is “unwanted,” but because Allah created the body with rhythms, and the religion is built with mercy toward those rhythms.
In other words: Islam honors the body by not demanding a form of worship that is not required in that state.
It honors the heart by keeping the door of remembrance open.
A Qur’anic anchor: Allah does not burden beyond capacity
One of the clearest realities the Qur’an repeats is that Allah knows what a human being can carry, and does not ask what is impossible.
Allah describes the religion as guidance and ease, not as a project of self‑harm.
So when your body is in a state where prayer is not required, the goal is not to “compensate” out of panic.
The goal is to stay turned toward Allah with what is actually possible today.
Orientation is not a scoreboard.
It is a direction.
How ḥayḍ is honored: permission, not exile
This is one of the quiet mercies that took me time to feel properly.
A pause is built into the system.
Not as an error.
Not as a demotion.
But as an acknowledgement.
Menstruation is treated as a real state with real rules.
That in itself is honor.
It says:
Your body is not an obstacle to faith.
Your biology is not a spiritual embarrassment.
Your worship is not reduced to output.
What practices are recommended today (Eid, while menstruating)
Different schools of Islamic law have different details about what is permissible in menstruation.
If you want exact rulings for your situation, it is always best to check a trusted scholar you follow.
But the spirit is consistent across the tradition: when one door is closed temporarily, many other doors remain open.
Here are practices that are widely understood as meaningful and safe choices for today.
First: keep remembrance close.
Dhikr can be simple.
It does not need intensity.
It needs sincerity.
Repeat one phrase slowly as you move through the morning.
Let it be the thread running through the day.
Second: make duʿā’ real.
Duʿā’ is not a performance.
It is closeness.
It is need.
It is the heart telling the truth in front of Allah.
Third: send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ.
If you do not know a long formula, even a short one repeated with love is a kind of light.
Fourth: do a concrete act of good.
Eid is not only celebration.
It is also generosity.
A small charity.
A warm message.
A meal shared.
A kind word.
A repaired relationship.
This is worship that lands in the world.
Fifth: honor the day outwardly too.
If you have the energy, do the human part of Eid.
Wash.
Wear something clean.
Make your space beautiful.
Prepare something small.
Reach out.
Let the celebration include you, even if you are not praying.
A small Eid Fajr orientation ritual (7 minutes)
Think of this as a bridge.
Not a replacement for ṣalāh, and not a performance for anyone.
Just a short loop that brings you back to reality, back to meaning, and back to God.
Start with what you have.
If you only have two minutes, do two minutes.
If you have seven minutes, do seven.
First, make the body a little quieter.
Wash your hands and face.
Drink some water.
Sit down.
Let your jaw and shoulders unclench.
This is not “wudū’,” but it is a reset.
It tells the nervous system: we are safe enough to be present.
Then set a simple intention.
You can say it in your own language.
Something like:
“I am turning toward Allah with what is possible for me right now.”
After that, choose one short dhikr phrase and let it become a gentle breath‑anchor.
Pick one and repeat it slowly, as if you are laying down a steady track:
SubḥānAllāh.
Alḥamdulillāh.
Allāhu akbar.
When the mind drifts, you simply return.
That returning is the point.
Then make duʿā’ simple and honest.
Do not try to sound holy.
Speak like a real person speaking to the One who already knows.
If you want a structure, you can use four lines:
“Ya Allah, thank You for this morning.”
“Ya Allah, help me stay steady today.”
“Ya Allah, protect me from my own impulses and from needless harm.”
“Ya Allah, guide me on the straight path.”
Finally, end with one tiny act that makes worship concrete.
Not big.
Not heroic.
Just real.
Send a warm message to someone who will be alone today.
Give a small amount of charity.
Clean one small corner of your space.
Feed yourself well.
Do one thing that brings order, mercy, or honesty into the world.
Why this is aligned with reality and feedback
This is what I keep learning in practice: the soul is not separate from the organism.
When the body is strained, the mind narrows.
When the mind narrows, the heart struggles to hold complexity.
And when the heart loses orientation, the ego rushes in with noise.
Ṣalāh interrupts that spiral several times a day.
It returns attention.
It cuts through momentum.
It reminds you that you are not the center.
When ṣalāh pauses, you can still keep the same logic alive in a smaller form:
repetition (dhikr),
direction (intention),
relationship (duʿā’),
and embodiment (a small act of good).
It is not about doing more.
It is about staying connected to the reference point.
If guilt shows up, treat it like weather
On days like this, guilt often appears wearing religious language.
It says you are falling behind.
It says you are not real enough.
It says you are missing out.
But guilt is not always guidance.
Sometimes it is just the nervous system looking for control.
So name it gently.
“This is guilt.”
Then soften it.
“I do not need to fight this feeling.”
Then return to one small act of orientation.
Eid, even from the margins
If you are not praying today, you are not outside of Islam.
You are inside the human reality that Islam already accounts for.
Your Lord is still your Lord.
Guidance is still guidance.
And the straight path is still available in small steps.
Eid mubārak.
May Allah accept what is possible from you today, and expand what becomes possible tomorrow.
If you only do one thing today:
Sit for one minute.
Put your hand on your chest.
And say, simply: “Ya Allah, guide me.

title: The Sixth Joint Point: When Deconstruction Requires Orientation
text:
Photo by Patrick von der Wehd on Unsplash
A response to Mind & Mythos: Psychology Finally Has a Unifying Framework
Gregg Henriques’ Unified Theory of Knowledge is one of the more serious attempts in recent decades to give psychology a coherent foundation. His four joint points, Matter, Life, Mind, Culture, trace the ascending arc of complexity, each level folding back on the one beneath it and beginning to regulate from a new vantage. It is an elegant ontology of emergence. It earns its ambition.
But it leaves something unresolved. Not a gap in the theory so much as a silence at its edge. The framework explains how consciousness arose. It does not address what happens when consciousness turns back on itself, and finds nothing there.
The Fifth Joint Point: When Justification Collapses
Henriques’ Justification Hypothesis describes how human beings stabilize their behavior through shared reasoning. Culture, on this account, is a network of explanations that holds action in place. We act, and then we explain why, and the explanation becomes real enough to shape the next action.
What neuroscience and contemplative traditions have both, independently, observed is that this sequence is reversed from how it feels. The nervous system moves first. Justification arrives after, a reconstruction, a narrative the mind assembles to preserve the sense that someone was in charge.
In Buddhist phenomenology, this becomes visible through sustained practice. As attention refines, the practitioner begins to notice the machinery: sensation arises, movement follows, and the story of why appears only in the wake. And eventually, even the witness, the one supposedly watching all of this, is revealed to be part of the same process. Not a subject observing events, but another event.
This is the Fifth Joint Point: not an ascent to a new level of complexity, but the collapse of the fourth. Culture discovers that it was consciousness narrating to itself. The self becomes transparent. Justification, seen clearly, dissolves its own authority.
The Problem With Collapse
Most accounts treat this as resolution. As though seeing through the illusion were the same as being free of it.
But it is not.
Because even after the self-model has collapsed, the body is still here. Decisions still unfold. Actions accumulate into a life, and that life has consequences. The absence of a sovereign self does not produce the absence of responsibility, it intensifies it. There is no one to blame, and yet causation continues. The question of how to act does not go away when the actor is revealed as fiction. It becomes more urgent.
What fills the space left by the dissolved self is not clarity. It is drift. And drift, over time, compounds.
The Sixth Joint Point: Constraint After Dissolution
The transition that follows deconstruction is not further dissolution. It is not a return to naivety. It is something more specific: the reintroduction of constraint into a system that has lost its center.
By this point, several things are already known. The self is not sovereign. Perception is constructed. Justification is unreliable. These are no longer philosophical positions, they are direct observations, repeated and verified. And yet behavior still has to be organized. Consequences still have to be navigated. A life still has to be lived across time, not just moment to moment.
The question that emerges is not who am I but what regulates a system that can no longer regulate itself through self-reference?
The Failure of the Obvious Candidates
There are not many options, and most of them fail.
The self is already disqualified, exposed as recursive, post-hoc, and unstable under pressure. Raw feedback from reality exists, but it arrives late, arrives ambiguously, and corrects rather than guides. You can learn from consequences, but you cannot navigate by them in real time. And pure awareness, the great promise of contemplative traditions, clarifies perception without organizing action. It reduces illusion. It does not produce discipline, or long-range alignment, or the capacity to act consistently when the cost is high and the reward is distant.
Something else is needed, not a belief, but a structure. Not a story, but a reference point that does not depend on the self to hold.
What Religion Actually Does
This is where historical religious systems become legible in a new way, not as metaphysics to be evaluated, but as engineering to be understood.
Traditions like Islam do something structurally precise. They introduce a reference external to the self and make that reference non-negotiable. They interrupt self-referential loops at fixed intervals, not when the practitioner feels ready, but on schedule, regardless of inner state. They embed constraint into the body through repeated, embodied practice. And they align action not just across moments but across a lifetime, across generations, across a horizon the self cannot see.
Whether or not one accepts the metaphysical claims, the functional architecture is coherent. It stabilizes a system that, left to its own devices, fragments. The external reference, God, in the theistic framing, is not primarily a comfort. It is a solution to a structural problem.
A Different Question
At this stage, the question is no longer is this belief true in the correspondence sense. The question becomes: does this orientation successfully organize a system that cannot organize itself?
This is not a retreat from rigor. It is a more demanding form of it. Because it requires testing, not once, but over time, through practice, through friction, through the accumulation of a lived life. The framework cannot be evaluated from outside. It can only be evaluated from within, which is what makes it uncomfortable for a certain kind of rationalism.
But the discomfort is not evidence against it. It is what the test requires.
From Authorship to Alignment
The Fifth Joint Point dismantled the illusion of control.
The Sixth confronts what replaces it, not with another illusion, but with a different relationship to constraint. Not self-authorship, but alignment. Not certainty, but structured commitment in the absence of certainty.
Light a flame. Feel the warmth. Notice the story forming, and notice how it arrives after the fact, assembled in the wake of what the body already did. This is not a problem to be solved. It is a feature of the system.
But then: choose alignment anyway. Choose it not because you fully understand, not because the metaphysics is settled, but because action still shapes reality, and a life lived without orientation compounds in the wrong direction.
The Unified Theory of Knowledge maps emergence beautifully. To complete it, it must also account for what comes after insight, for the question that arises not at the beginning of the journey, but at its most clarifying moment:
What is worthy of guiding a system that cannot guide itself?
That is not the end of inquiry. It is where the serious work begins.

title: Collapse as Loss of Coordination: Lessons from 1177 B.C.
text:
This is a piece I originally wrote in September 2025. I’ve revisited it now, not just to clean up the language, but because my understanding of collapse has shifted. What follows is less a prediction, and more a clarification of what I think we are actually looking at when systems begin to fail.
“Collapse” is a dramatic word. It suggests rupture, spectacle, something unmistakable. Sirens, smoke, a clear before and after.
But most systems do not fail like that.
They drift.
A shipment arrives late. A signal is missed. A decision that should have been revised is quietly maintained. The system continues to operate, but something subtle has changed: it is no longer adjusting properly to reality. From the inside, it still feels stable. From a distance, the pattern is already loosening.
This is what becomes visible when you look closely at the Late Bronze Age collapse, often summarized through Eric Cline’s 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed. The title suggests a moment. The reality is something else entirely.
That world did not disappear overnight. It lost its ability to hold together.
The Late Bronze Age was, in many ways, a success story. Kingdoms were linked through diplomacy, trade networks stretched across regions, and elites shared a common language of power and prestige. Copper moved from Cyprus, grain from Egypt, correspondence between rulers addressed each other as “brother.” It was a tightly integrated system, sophisticated and efficient.
And that was precisely the problem.
The more tightly a system is coupled, the less room it has to absorb disturbance. Efficiency reduces slack. Slack is what allows systems to bend.
So when disruptions came, droughts, earthquakes, raids, interruptions in trade, they did not remain local. They propagated. Each shock interacted with others. Pressure accumulated.
But even that is not the core of the story.
Shocks alone do not cause collapse. Systems encounter stress all the time. The critical failure is this:
They stop being able to coordinate a response.
Instead of adapting, systems begin to reinforce themselves. Leaders double down on control. Narratives of stability persist even as conditions change. Signals become harder to interpret, trust erodes, and responses fragment.
From the outside, collapse can look sudden. From within, it is a long erosion of coherence.
There is a tendency, especially in contemporary discourse, to soften collapse into something almost comforting. A transformation. A release. A natural renewal.
There is some truth in that. Systems do reorganize. New forms do emerge.
But this framing is incomplete.
Collapse is not inherently regenerative. It can just as easily produce prolonged instability, loss of knowledge, fragmentation, or violence. History does not guarantee that breakdown leads to something better. It only guarantees that the previous pattern cannot be maintained.
A more precise way to understand it is this:
Collapse creates the conditions for reconfiguration. It does not determine the outcome.
What makes this pattern difficult to see is that it repeats across scales.
You can observe it in ecosystems, where periods of growth are followed by saturation, then disturbance, then reorganization. You can observe it in economies, where expansion gives way to fragility when everything becomes “always on.”
And you can observe it in the body.
Burnout follows the same structure. There is a phase of expansion, effort, output, engagement. Then saturation, stress layered on stress, reduced recovery, diminishing resilience. Eventually, something gives. The system can no longer sustain the pattern. What follows is not collapse as spectacle, but collapse as refusal. The body stops.
What happens next depends on whether reconfiguration is allowed.
There are even built-in rhythms that reflect this logic. The menstrual cycle, for example, is not just biological, it is regulatory. Expansion, saturation, release, renewal. A system that periodically lets go maintains flexibility. A system that tries to suppress release accumulates pressure.
The principle is consistent:
Systems that cannot release become brittle. Brittle systems break.
When you look at the present through this lens, the parallels are difficult to ignore.
Modern civilization is highly interconnected. Food systems depend on global logistics. Energy systems depend on complex supply chains. Financial systems are tightly linked. Information flows instantly.
This produces extraordinary capability. It also creates conditions where disturbances travel far and fast.
A drought in one region influences prices elsewhere. A disruption in a port affects production across continents. A cyberattack can cascade into physical consequences. None of this is new in principle. What is new is the speed and scale at which it occurs.
But again, the decisive factor is not disturbance alone.
It is whether systems can still coordinate under pressure.
When coordination begins to fail, signals become unreliable. Institutions struggle to respond coherently. Narratives no longer align behavior. What you get is not immediate collapse, but fragmentation, multiple responses, no shared direction.
This points to something I did not fully understand when I first wrote this.
Systems are not only held together by material flows, resources, energy, infrastructure. They are also held together by orientation.
Shared assumptions. Shared meanings. A sense of direction.
When that weakens, coordination becomes harder, even if the material system is still intact. People begin to act according to different models of reality. Decisions diverge. Coherence erodes.
This is also why “guidance” matters as a practical systems function, not as a moral add-on. When people and institutions have a clearer way to interpret signals, choose priorities, and adjust behavior, the system retains the ability to coordinate under stress. When guidance fragments, even small disturbances can produce outsized confusion, because there is no shared frame for what counts as information, what counts as a response, and what can be released.
In that sense, collapse is not only physical. It is also a breakdown in how reality is interpreted and acted upon collectively.
So the question is not whether systems will face stress. They always do.
The real question is what happens when they do.
There are, broadly speaking, two trajectories.
One is combustion. Systems become rigid, delays in adaptation accumulate, and when change finally occurs, it is abrupt and destabilizing.
The other is something closer to composting. Release is allowed earlier. Adjustments happen in smaller increments. The system reorganizes without fully breaking apart.
The difference is not the presence of pressure. It is how the system handles it.
Whether it can let go.
Whether it can adapt.
Whether it can still coordinate.
What this implies, at a practical level, is less dramatic than the word “collapse” suggests.
Resilience is not built through grand interventions, but through design choices that appear almost mundane. Systems that maintain buffers, time, energy, resources, can absorb disturbance. Systems that reduce tight coupling limit cascade effects. Systems that shorten feedback loops detect stress before it becomes irreversible.
Perhaps most importantly, systems that normalize endings, projects, assumptions, commitments, create space for renewal.
And at the most basic level, systems that treat rest as structural rather than optional maintain their capacity to function.
The point is not to predict a singular moment of collapse.
It is to recognize a pattern.
Systems expand. They saturate. They struggle to adapt. They either reorganize or they break.
The difference is not fate.
It is whether release and coordination remain possible.
History, ecology, and the body all point in the same direction:
Systems that cannot let go, eventually fail.
Systems that can, have a chance, not a guarantee, but a real possibility, to reorganize into something that holds.

title: The Living Fractal (Rewritten, 2026)
text:
A note on origin
This piece began as something else.
I first wrote it in early 2025, at a time when my sense of reality was unstable. I had just come out of burnout, and the frameworks I relied on, about identity, control, even perception itself, were no longer holding together. I wasn’t writing from clarity. I was writing to track what was happening to me, because it felt too complex and too intense to ignore.
Looking back, that version of this work was raw. It leaned heavily into deconstruction, questioning everything, dissolving assumptions, pulling apart the structures that shape how we see the world. That phase mattered. It showed me how much of what we call “reality” is not directly perceived, but constructed through layers of interpretation.
But it was incomplete.
So this is a rewrite. Not just a cleaner version, but a more grounded one, shaped by everything I’ve learned since.
There is a moment when your models of reality stop working.
Not dramatically. Not all at once. More like a quiet misalignment. Things still function on the surface, but something underneath has shifted. What used to feel stable starts to feel slightly off. Explanations don’t quite land. You notice gaps, delays, inconsistencies. At first, it’s subtle enough to ignore.
Then it isn’t.
What I came to understand is that this isn’t just a psychological experience. It’s structural.
We don’t perceive reality directly. We build internal models of it, compressed, simplified, constrained by the limits of our bodies and our attention. Most of the time, those models are “good enough.” They allow us to function, to coordinate, to move through the world without constantly re-evaluating everything.
But when the environment changes, or when pressure accumulates, those models can start to drift. And when they drift far enough, the system, whether it’s a person, a relationship, or a society, loses its ability to adjust properly.
From the inside, it can still feel stable.
From a distance, the pattern is already loosening.
This is not just something that happens to individuals. It shows up across scales.
In ecosystems, in economies, in civilizations, you see the same rhythm repeat. Systems expand. They grow, connect, optimize. Over time, they become more efficient, but also more tightly coupled. There’s less slack, less redundancy, less room to absorb disturbance.
Then pressure builds.
Not necessarily from one cause, but from many small ones interacting: resource strain, environmental shifts, misaligned incentives, delayed feedback. Each on its own is manageable. Together, they start to synchronize.
And then something changes.
Not always a collapse in the dramatic sense. More often, a loss of coordination. Signals become harder to interpret. Responses fragment. Different parts of the system start acting according to different assumptions. The system continues, but it no longer moves as one.
That’s when coherence begins to erode.
I recognized this pattern because I had lived it in my own body.
Burnout is often described as exhaustion, but that’s not quite precise. It’s closer to a system-level refusal. There is a period of expansion, effort, output, engagement. Then saturation, stress layered on stress, recovery becomes insufficient, the system tightens.
And then, eventually, it stops cooperating.
Not as a choice, but as a limit.
The body withdraws capacity because it can no longer sustain the pattern it was maintaining.
What happens after that depends on whether you allow reconfiguration.
If you resist it, if you try to force the old pattern back into place, you prolong instability. If you allow it, something else can emerge. Not instantly, not cleanly, but gradually.
This is where I began to understand something that was missing in my earlier thinking.
Collapse is not inherently meaningful. It does not guarantee renewal. It simply creates the conditions where renewal becomes possible.
The outcome depends on what happens next.
There are systems that break under pressure.
And there are systems that adapt.
The difference is not strength. It’s flexibility.
More specifically, it’s whether the system knows how to release.
You can see this in the most basic biological rhythms. The body is not designed for constant output. It operates in cycles, expansion, saturation, release, renewal. Even the menstrual cycle reflects this logic. There is a phase of building, a phase of holding, a phase of release, and then a phase of recovery.
If you interrupt that release, if you try to override it, you don’t eliminate the cycle. You distort it. Pressure accumulates elsewhere.
The same principle applies everywhere.
Systems that cannot release become brittle. And brittle systems don’t bend. They break.
When you look at the present through this lens, certain patterns become difficult to ignore.
Modern systems are highly interconnected. Food, energy, finance, information, everything is linked. This creates extraordinary capability. It also means that disturbances travel faster and further than before.
But again, disturbance itself is not the decisive factor.
The real question is whether coordination holds.
Because systems are not only held together by material flows, resources, infrastructure, logistics. They are also held together by orientation. Shared assumptions. Shared ways of interpreting what is happening and what should be done.
When that begins to fragment, even small disruptions can produce disproportionate effects.
Not because the system is physically gone, but because it no longer knows how to respond coherently.
This is where my understanding shifted most.
Earlier, I treated collapse almost as a natural transformation, something that could be softened into a kind of release, even something regenerative.
There is some truth in that.
But it’s not guaranteed.
Collapse can also mean prolonged instability. Loss of knowledge. Fragmentation. Suffering. History is clear on that.
So the more precise way to understand it is this:
Collapse does not determine the outcome. It only removes the old pattern.
What replaces it depends on whether coordination, adaptation, and orientation can be restored.
That has practical implications.
Resilience is not built through dramatic interventions. It’s built through small, often unremarkable design choices.
It shows up in whether there is buffer, time, energy, margin.
It shows up in whether everything is tightly coupled, or whether failures can remain local.
It shows up in how quickly feedback is detected and acted upon.
And it shows up in whether systems allow endings, whether they can let go of patterns that no longer fit.
At the most basic level, it shows up in whether rest is treated as optional, or as structural.
Because rest is not the opposite of function.
It is what makes function possible.
So this is where I stand now, looking back at where this began.
Not in a place of certainty, but in a clearer understanding of the pattern.
Systems expand. They saturate. They struggle to adapt. They either reorganize, or they break.
The difference is not fate.
It is whether they can still:
adjust,
release,
and remain coordinated under pressure.
This work, The Living Fractal, is no longer about dissolving everything.
It is about seeing clearly enough to remain stable
without becoming rigid.
To stay open to revision
without losing structure.
To understand reality not as something fixed,
but as something that must be continuously
perceived, tested, and realigned.
Not once.
But over and over again.
If you read this carefully, you’ll notice something:
This is no longer “searching.”
This is orientation.
That shift matters….

title: Breaking Conditioned Perception
subtitle: Without Losing Your Ground
text:
A reflection on deconstruction, instability, and what actually helps
This is a piece I originally wrote in February 2025.
At the time, I was going through a period of intense internal change. My sense of reality had started to shift, and many of the assumptions I had relied on, about identity, perception, and truth, no longer felt stable. I was questioning everything, not as a philosophical exercise, but because I could no longer take my own perception for granted.
Looking back, that phase contained real insight. But it also contained a misunderstanding that pushed me close to losing my grounding.
This is a rewrite of that piece, keeping what was true, but correcting what was incomplete.
There is something deeply unsettling about realizing that your perception is not a direct window onto reality.
We tend to assume that what we see, feel, and think reflects the world as it is. But if you look closely, that assumption starts to break down. The brain does not passively receive reality, it constructs a model of it. It filters, predicts, and compresses information into something manageable.
Most of the time, this works well. It allows us to move through the world without constantly questioning everything.
But once you begin to see that your experience is constructed, something shifts.
You start to notice how much of what you took as “given” is shaped by conditioning, by culture, language, memory, and expectation. Even things that feel fundamental, like the sense of self or the flow of time, become open to question.
That realization can be liberating.
It can also be destabilizing.
In my earlier version of this work, I treated deconstruction almost as an end in itself. The goal, implicitly, was to strip away conditioning until nothing remained, no assumptions, no fixed identity, no ground.
At the time, this felt like clarity.
In reality, it was incomplete.
Because a system cannot function without some form of structure.
The self, for example, is not a fixed entity in the way we often imagine it. It is a constructed model, a way of organizing experience, memory, and action. But recognizing that it is constructed does not mean it should be eliminated.
It means it should be understood.
When I pushed too far into deconstruction, questioning not only beliefs, but perception itself, I began to notice something important. The sense of self would dissolve under scrutiny, but it would also return.
Again and again.
At first, I interpreted that as something to overcome. I thought I needed to go further, to see through it more completely.
But the more I pushed, the less stable I became.
There were moments where perception felt too fast, too open. Too much was coming in at once, without the usual filtering. My thoughts became more abstract, more intense. At times, I genuinely wondered whether I was losing touch with reality.
That was not clarity.
That was a system under strain.
What I understand now is much simpler, and much more grounded.
Perception is constructed, but it is constructed under constraint.
The self is a model, but it is a necessary one.
You can see through it, but you still need it to function.
Deconstruction, on its own, is not a stable state. It is a phase.
If you remove structure faster than you rebuild it, the system destabilizes. Not because you are “doing something wrong” morally, but because you are removing the very mechanisms that allow you to stay oriented.
That was the mistake I made.
There is also a common misconception that reinforces this.
In some interpretations of contemplative traditions, you encounter the idea that the goal is to transcend the self completely, to reach a state of “no-self” and remain there. When taken literally, this can lead to a subtle but dangerous conclusion: that grounding, identity, and structure are obstacles to be removed.
In practice, that does not hold.
Even if the sense of self dissolves temporarily, it returns. It has to. Without it, you cannot act, relate, or coordinate your behavior in the world.
The aim is not to eliminate the self.
It is to stop mistaking it for something fixed and absolute.
That is a very different task.
Another thing I underestimated at the time was the role of the body.
When you destabilize your cognitive models, your nervous system still needs regulation. If you stay only in abstraction, thinking, analyzing, questioning, you lose contact with the signals that keep you grounded.
What helped me most during that period was not more thinking.
It was simple things:
walking, being outside, returning to physical sensation, allowing time for things to settle.
Those are not small details.
They are what keep the system intact while it reorganizes.
So if there is one thing I would correct from my earlier writing, it is this:
Breaking conditioned perception is not about removing everything you rely on.
It is about seeing clearly where your models come from, how they shape your experience, and where they fail, while still maintaining enough structure to remain functional.
There is a difference between:
Questioning your assumptions and…
Removing your ability to orient yourself.
That distinction matters.
What happens when you do this more carefully is not that reality disappears.
It becomes more precise.
You begin to see that:
perception is not neutral
but it is not arbitrary either
your experience is shaped
but also constrained
And within those constraints, you can refine how you see and how you act.
Looking back, I don’t regret that phase.
It showed me something real.
But I also see clearly now that intensity without grounding is not depth. It is instability.
The work is not to go as far as possible, as fast as possible.
The work is to:
see,
test,
integrate,
and stabilize.
Because in the end, clarity is not measured by how much you can deconstruct.
It is measured by whether you can remain oriented
while seeing more of what is actually there.
For me, that orientation is increasingly built through practice: returning to something steady, embodied, and repeatable, even when the mind wants to spiral into abstraction. In Islam, that steadiness looks less like chasing “more insight” and more like guidance in the simple sense, being directed, on purpose, day by day. The more I commit to prayer, grounding routines, and a lived ethic, the less this work feels like dissolving reality, and the more it feels like learning how to see clearly without losing my way.
